newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: E.Asian Grain-Taiwan pork woes to trim corn prices.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grain-Taiwan pork woes to trim corn prices.

text.p: Corn prices are likely to drop further in the wake of the foot-and-mouth disease which crippled Taiwan's pork industry, traders said on Monday.
"It will translate to lower corn prices," predicted a dealer with a major flour company in Manila.
"Corn users who have been using less costly wheat as a substitute will now go back to corn," he said.

The price of the May corn contract on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) fell 4-1/2 U.S. cents on Friday to end at US$3.00-1/4 a bushel due to concerns about lost sales of U.S. corn to Taiwan, one of its biggest customers.

But one corn dealer for a European commodity house in Manila said any fall in Taiwanese imports may be offset by increased consumption by U.S. hog raisers who stand to benefit from the indefinite ban slapped by Japan on Taiwan's pork products.

Taiwanese traders said the ban on pork exports to its main markets in Japan and South Korea could result in a decline in corn imports of about 1.2 million tonnes, one-fifth of the country's total corn imports.
Japanese traders estimated Taiwan may call off up to 500,000 tonnes of U.S. corn imports in the next few weeks.
"The export ban will surely cut Taiwanese corn demand in the near term," a corn trader at a major trade house in Tokyo said.
"Some pork breeders in Japan will try to boost output," the trader said. "But their pork production growth will be limited because of environmental reasons."
Dealers in South Korea, though, shrugged off the concerns over corn prices, saying the fall in Chicago futures on Friday indicated the market had already absorbed the news on Taiwan's pork industry.
They said Korea's National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF) would probably buy about 85,000 tonnes of Chinese corn this week for September delivery.
"Some buyers will move into the market to cover their needs," a trader at a Seoul-based foreign trading house said.

Japanese corn buyers ignored the news on Taiwan and finished buying 90 percent of its April/June requirements of U.S. corn, traders said. U.S. corn premiums for Japan were quoted at about 95 U.S. cents a bushel over the CBOT May contract.
"It's too early to boost buying for the July/September shipments. We'd like to wait for better timing," another corn trader in Tokyo said.
China was still talking with Japanese importers on corn sales, but any deal could not be confirmed yet, traders said.

South Korean buyers continued to express a preference for Chinese corn due to cheaper prices and faster shipment from the nearby Chinese port of Dalian. The Koreans have bought about 934,500 tonnes of Chinese origins since January.
Taiwanese traders said they also expected to see wheat buyers placing tenders for up to 68,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat within the next two weeks.

The NLCF trader said freight rates from the Pacific Northwest rose to $15.00-$16.00 a tonne from $14.50 last week because of rising demand for grain vessels. U.S. Gulf rates also climbed to $25.00-$26.00 a tonne from $24.50 the previous week.
